summary:
Lovejoy and Howard frame enterprise AI agent work through U.S. health insurance deployments, arguing lessons transfer to any regulated industry where process compliance matters and decisions directly affect lives. They open with a familiar POC arc: two engineers over four weeks connect an agent to application, control plane, data plane, and model provider layers, pulling offline and online data. Results look strong and finance, the CMO, and sales are pleased. Everyone assumes the AI was the hard part.

The next day's productionization meeting surfaces the real difficulties: audit trails, sensitive-data handling, escalation, and zero trust.

Howard argues an audit trail under SOC 2, HITRUST, or HIPAA must be a legal-grade chain of evidence, not a developer log. He recommends an immutable, append-only timestamp event log as the single source of truth, which makes auditability automatic but makes reads harder, requiring caching or snapshots. PHI is stored separately in schema-driven object storage; events hold only references. This lets developers debug agents without seeing PHI, enables zero-trust enforcement at the object store, mitigates prompt injection via the lethal trifecta, and keeps data inside the customer's environment.

Escalation is handled by defining agents as encompassing both humans and LLMs, so any LLM-actionable step can be handed to a human, with shared context methods mapping to prompts or UIs. The three primitives together yield privacy-preserving evaluation almost as a byproduct: the ledger allows replaying exact states, human-agent equivalency produces eval scores by diffing human and LLM outputs, and object storage enables eval on production data without exposing it. The talk closes by framing architecture as choosing what stays simple and treating constraints as foundations, then rebuilding up to POC accuracy.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: In regulated enterprises, productionization requirements (audit trail, sensitive data, escalation, zero trust) dominate AI agent design, not model accuracy.
An audit trail under SOC 2, HITRUST, or HIPAA is a legal-grade chain of evidence, not a developer log.
An immutable append-only event log makes auditability a property of the storage model, trading easier writes for harder reads.
Separating PHI in schema-driven object storage from event references enables debugging without PHI access, zero-trust enforcement, and data that stays in the customer's environment.
Separation of data and orchestration streams mitigates prompt injection by preventing agents from combining untrusted data with sensitive data in the same process.
Treating humans and models uniformly as agents is the foundation for predictable escalation and shared context mapping to prompts or UIs.
Evaluation emerges as a byproduct of the three primitives: ledger replay, human/LLM diffing, and in-environment eval on production data.
Taking constraints seriously first and rebuilding toward accuracy yields resilient architecture; bolting requirements onto a POC yields brittle systems.
Patterns from finance, defense, and big tech already solve many of these problems and can be combined for AI agent systems.
Distinguish a legal-grade audit trail from a typical developer log.

sections.title: Introductions and why healthcare is hard
sections.summary: Lovejoy and Howard introduce themselves and Anterior, framing healthcare AI as hard because of process, compliance, and real-world impact, and noting lessons transfer to finance, defense, and government work.

sections.title: The enterprise POC scenario
sections.summary: A typical POC: two engineers, four weeks, building an administrative healthcare workflow that connects to application, control plane, data plane, and model provider layers, pulling data from a data lake and the application layer, offline and online.

sections.title: Success in the room, hard part not yet done
sections.summary: The demo lands: accuracy hit, fast, cheap, and finance, the chief medical officer, and sales are excited. But everyone assumes the AI itself was the challenge, ignoring what productionization will require.

sections.title: The next day's compliance meeting
sections.summary: A productionization meeting surfaces hard questions: who can see the audit trail, how is sensitive data handled and bounded, who approves decisions and escalates to clinicians, can untrusted data manipulate the model, and how do integrations to Epic and Salesforce work. The talk focuses on the first four.

sections.title: Audit trail as a legal record, not a developer log
sections.summary: Howard reframes an audit trail under SOC 2, HITRUST, or HIPAA as a complete, legal-grade chain of evidence covering every agent action, data access, and authorization. He recommends an immutable, append-only timestamp event log as the single source of truth across parallel agents.

sections.title: Trade-off of the immutable event log
sections.summary: The append-only event sourcing pattern makes writes trivial and auditability automatic but makes reads harder, requiring caching or snapshots. In healthcare, post-hoc reinterpretations of a patient's journey are normal, and ephemeral computed projections over the event log make those views easy.

sections.title: Shape of healthcare data and schema-driven object storage
sections.summary: PHI is complex, unstructured and structured, large (often over a megabyte), strictly access-controlled, and sometimes confined to on-prem VPCs. Schema-driven object storage fits that shape and pairs with the event log because events hold only references to the stored blobs, not the data itself.

sections.title: Debugging without seeing PHI and zero trust
sections.summary: Storing events separately from PHI lets developers retrace agent steps and observe orchestration without access to protected health information, separating observability from the data. The object store becomes the natural place to enforce zero-trust access, with agents bearing tokens to retrieve data at need.

sections.title: Zero trust and prompt injection mitigation
sections.summary: Object storage segregated from the event stream enforces zero trust by keeping data at point of use and preventing free flow through the system. This same separation helps solve the lethal trifecta: an agent cannot access two data sources within the same process, so untrusted data cannot be combined with sensitive data to exfiltrate it.

sections.title: Escalation when you cannot predict it
sections.summary: Escalation timing and triggers are dynamic, and humans and LLMs process context differently. Treating humans and LLMs as the same kind of agent means any LLM-actionable step can be handed to a human, and downstream steps don't care which acted upstream. Shared context methods map to either prompts or UIs, so the same action surfaces appropriately for either actor.

sections.title: Why evals are hard here
sections.summary: Evals are difficult because LLMs are non-deterministic, offline datasets may not represent production, and data drifts over time. In regulated settings, bringing production data to external eval pipelines is also often disallowed.

sections.title: Evaluation as a byproduct of the primitives
sections.summary: The three primitives yield effective privacy-preserving evals almost automatically: the immutable ledger lets you replay the exact system state and measure the precise impact of prompt, model, or code changes; human-agent equivalency lets you diff human and LLM outputs as eval scores; object storage lets you run evals on production data inside the customer's environment without ever exposing the data to the agent's compute.

sections.title: Architecture as choosing what stays simple
sections.summary: Lovejoy recaps the four architectural principles (immutable ledger of actions, orchestration-adjacent object storage, human-agent equivalency, evals as a first-class property) and frames architecture as taking constraints seriously, choosing what should stay simple, and accepting that other things become hard. Many of the underlying patterns already exist in finance, defense, and big tech and can be combined for AI systems.

sections.title: Where it goes wrong, and where it goes right
sections.summary: It goes wrong when a POC with strong accuracy is treated as a foundation and enterprise requirements are strapped on after the fact, producing brittle, hard-to-generalize systems. It goes right when production-ready, scaled enterprise constraints are treated as architectural principles from the start, and the team rebuilds up to POC accuracy on those primitives.

limitations: Reads are more difficult with append-only event logs and require patterns like caching or snapshots.
The talk focuses on only four productionization concerns; questions about untrusted data manipulating models, ongoing performance, and integrations (Epic, Salesforce) are deferred.
Escalation timing and rules cannot always be predicted in advance, making dynamic enforcement necessary.
quantitativeClaims: Two engineers over four weeks to build the POC.
A single piece of healthcare data can easily exceed one megabyte.
